newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fannie Mae to target Japanese retail investors.
newsitem.headline: Fannie Mae to target Japanese retail investors.

text.p: The Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae) said on Tuesday that it was planning to develop a programme to raise funds from Japanese retail investors, and was also considering offering Euroyen bonds.
It would be the first Fannie Mae retail programme to target private investors outside of the United States.
"We're very well aware of (Japanese investors') appetite for higher-yielding investments in yen," James Johnson, chief executive officer at Fannie Mae, told Reuters.
"We're a very high-quality issuer...with great liquidity," Johnson said. "We're looking very carefully at increasing opportunities to issue in yen."
Fannie Mae said it was planning to develop the programme by early 1997.
"It (the Japanese market) is an attraction for Fannie Mae," Linda Knight, senior vice president, told a news conference.
In June, Fannie Mae re-entered the yen bond market by issuing global bonds. Since then it has launched two yen-based issues, both in September.

Knight said Fannie Mae was planning to develop such a programme for retail investors in Japan as Japanese investors were showing significant interest in investing in high-quality securities with high liquidity, high yield and high credit ratings.

Underwriting sources here said retail investors have been investing heavily in higher-yield yen-based bonds, especially those in the samurai and Euroyen markets, seeking higher returns at a time of record low interest rates at home.
At this stage, Fannie Mae is planning to offer Euroyen bonds, although the scale of the issue has not yet been decided, Knight said.
Fannie Mae issues long-term debt to support its mortgage portfolio. At the current pace, it will issue approximately $80 billion to $85 billion worth of long-term debt in 1996.

Concerning U.S. interest rates, Timothy Howard, executive vice president, told the news conference that Fannie Mae had forecast that the yield of the key 30-year U.S. Treasury bond would move in a range of 6.0 and 7.0 percent in 1997. The benchmark 30-year T-bond was yielding 6.50 percent in Tokyo afternoon trade on Tuesday. -- Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3-3432-8785
